newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia backs Port Moresby over military crisis.
newsitem.headline: Australia backs Port Moresby over military crisis.

text.p: Australia on Tuesday backed the Papua New Guinea government's sacking of its rebellious defence chief, as regional leaders urged a speedy end to the impoverished South Pacific nation's political crisis.

Australian Prime Minister John Howard, in a special statement to parliament, said Canberra deplored sacked armed forces chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok's push against the government of Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan.
"We utterly deplore the attempts of the former commander-in-chief of the Papua New Guinea defence force to defy the authority of the duly-elected government of Papua New Guinea," Howard said.
"In the circumstances, the action taken by the prime minister of Papua New Guinea, Sir Julius Chan, to remove the head of the defence force was both understandable and justifiable."
Chan sacked Singirok late on Monday after the military chief demanded Chan's resignation over plans to use mercenaries in the war against secessionist rebels on Bougainville island.
Singirok on Tuesday accepted his dismissal but vowed to carry on his campaign against Chan.
New Zealand Foreign Minister Don McKinnon also backed Chan's actions, urging a speedy resolution to the crisis in Port Moresby and a peaceful solution to the Bougainville rebellion.
"It's going to take a few more days and some cool heads must prevail," McKinnon told New Zealand radio on Tuesday.
"Certainly our support (is) that the democratic government does remain and does retain authority."
"We've taken the stand that there has to be a political solution to this particular problem at Bougainville. It can't be a military solution."
McKinnon said he was concerned about the regional impact of the crisis in Papua New Guinea.
"You have to be concerned about the overall effect on regional stability," he said. "One hopes that cool heads have prevailed, that things will settle down."
The Papua New Guinea government decision to hire mercenaries, who Chan says will only be used as advisors, has sparked widespread condemnation from regional governments.
Howard stressed that Canberra remained strongly opposed to Chan's planned use of hired guns on Bougainville, 800 kilometres (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.
The pair held unannounced talks in Sydney earlier this month during which Howard repeated Australia's condemnation of any use of mercenaries.

"I made it very clear to him that Australia remained very strongly opposed to the use of mercenaries on Bougainville and that there would be if the use of those mercenaries in fact took place ... consequences of a serious kind so far as the relationship between Australia and New Guinea was concerned," Howard told parliament.

Australia is one of Port Moresby's major donors, providing about A$320 million (US$253 million) a year in aid. Howard said Australia was closely monitoring any threat to the thousands of Australians living in Papua New Guinea.
